-ilities: The quality attributes of a system - availability, scalability, reliability, security - that architects must design for deliberately.
AIaaS: AI as a Service - prebuilt AI capabilities (vision, language, agents) consumed over cloud APIs instead of built in-house.
AI governance: The policies, controls, and accountability that keep AI systems safe, legal, and aligned with company rules.
AIOps: Using AI to run IT operations - detecting incidents, predicting failures, and automating fixes.
Agent SDK: A standard software development kit for building AI agents, so every team builds them the same way.
Agentic AI: AI that doesn't just answer but takes actions - plans steps, calls tools, and completes tasks on its own.
Availability: The share of time a system stays up and usable, usually measured in nines (99.9% = three nines).
BluePlanet: IBM's reference architecture pattern for enterprise AI platforms.
Cloud 3.0: His term for the current cloud era: cloud as the operating layer for AI, after 1.0 (hosting) and 2.0 (cloud-native apps).
Context curator: An emerging role that manages what information an AI system sees - the quality of context decides the quality of answers.
Disaster recovery: The plan and infrastructure for bringing systems back after an outage or region failure.
Edge AI: Running AI models on devices close to users (stores, factories, phones) instead of a central cloud, for speed and privacy.
Embedding: Turning text into a list of numbers so similar meanings sit near each other - the basis of semantic search.
Enterprise Architect: The architect who looks across the whole organization's technology, not just one system.
Evaluation platform: Shared tooling that tests AI answers for correctness, safety, and quality before and after release.
GenAI: Generative AI - models that produce new text, images, or code rather than just classifying data.
GPT-OSS: OpenAI's open-weight model release (gpt-oss) that anyone can download and run themselves.
GPU: Graphics processing unit - the chip that trains and runs AI models; the scarce resource in AI infrastructure.
Guardrails as Code: Writing AI safety rules as versioned, testable code instead of documents nobody enforces.
Hallucination: When an AI model states something false with full confidence.
Inference: Running a trained model to get answers - the ongoing cost of AI, as opposed to one-time training.
Inference economy: The economics of running models at scale - every token costs money, so architecture decides the bill.
Inference gateway: A single front door that routes model requests to the right model, region, or provider.
KV cache: A memory trick that stores a model's earlier work so long conversations stay fast.
LangGraph: A framework for building multi-step AI agents as graphs of states and decisions, from the LangChain ecosystem.
LLM: Large language model - the engine behind chatbots and copilots.
MCP: Model Context Protocol - an open standard (from Anthropic) for connecting AI models to tools and data sources.
MCP Hub: A centralized, governed catalog of MCP servers so teams share vetted tools instead of wiring their own.
Multi-tenant: One platform serving many business units or customers, each isolated in its own logical space.
Paged attention: vLLM's memory-management technique that lets a GPU serve many more model requests at once.
Prompt registry: A central, versioned store of approved prompts so teams reuse and govern them instead of copying text around.
RAG: Retrieval-augmented generation - the model first looks up your documents, then answers from them.
RAG as a Service: RAG offered as a shared platform capability: any team brings documents, the platform handles chunking, search, and grounding.
Reliability: How consistently a system produces correct results over time, not just whether it is up.
Scalability: A system's ability to handle more users or work by adding resources rather than redesigning.
Solution Architect: The person who designs how a business problem becomes a working technical system.
TensorRT-LLM: NVIDIA's toolkit that compiles language models to run much faster on NVIDIA GPUs.
TOGAF: The Open Group Architecture Framework - the standard method for enterprise architecture work.
Token: The small chunk of text a model reads or writes; billing and limits are measured in tokens.
Unified tool catalog: One governed marketplace of every tool an agent may call, with ownership, cost, and policy attached.
vLLM: An open-source engine that serves language models fast by managing GPU memory efficiently.
Vector database: A database that stores embeddings and finds the most similar items - the search layer behind RAG.
watsonx: IBM's enterprise AI platform for building, governing, and running models.
Well-Architected Framework: Cloud vendors' published checklists (AWS, Azure) of design principles for secure, reliable, efficient systems.
Workflow automation: Software that runs multi-step business processes automatically, now increasingly with AI agents inside.
